title: The Review Board

post.author: u/depot_desk_edurne
post.title: I run the night desk at a council's refuse depot. At 01:00 all six bin crews were signed out of their app at once. At 06:00, 1,100 households were texted that their bin was missed. Every one of those bins had been emptied.

blocks.text: I'm Edurne, night supervisor at the council's refuse depot. At 00:00 I send six crews into the city centre, one bin lorry each. Each crew empties one street every 15 minutes: 24 streets by 06:00.

Each crew lead carries a phone with the council's crew app: a program, a set of instructions the phone follows. It runs unopened in a pocket. When the lorry reaches a street, the app marks it collected from the lorry's position. At 06:00 the council's computer texts every household on an unmarked street: "your bin was missed".

The app marks streets only while its crew is signed in, like the wristbands in Tokens. It goes in steps. First, the lead signs in at 00:00 with a staff number. That sign-in lasts a set time. Before it runs out, the app asks the council's computer to renew it; that's a refresh, and the time starts again. With no refresh, the sign-in ends, and the app marks nothing until the lead types a code from my desk.
A change is a new version of the app, or of the rules the council's computer follows. Two went out this week.
Before a change goes out, it gets a review, in steps. The team writes down what it will do. Two other engineers, the reviewers, read it and ask questions. Then they approve it or send it back.
On Tuesday 20 October at 14:00 the security change went out, from the council's security team: sign-ins now last 1 hour, not 24, so a lost phone is useless sooner. Its review approved it.

On Wednesday 21 October at 10:00, after Tuesday night's shift had ended, the app team's change went out. To save battery, the app now refreshes only when someone opens it, not every 15 minutes on its own. Its own review, which checks speed and battery, approved it.
Tuesday night ran with the security change alone. Every street was marked.
Wednesday night's shift began at 00:00 on Thursday 22 October. At 01:00 my desk phone rang six times in one minute. Each lead's phone had chimed: "Signed out. Ask the depot desk for a code."

A code takes me 15 minutes. I'm alone, with one phone line. I make the code on the desk computer, ring the lead back on the number we hold, and wait while they park somewhere safe to type it. I take crews in the order they called. They kept emptying bins.
Crew 1's night, from my desk's sign-in list, then the 06:00 texts by crew: households a street times streets unmarked.

00:00  crew 1  signed in
01:00  crew 1  signed out
01:15  crew 1  signed in, code
02:15  crew 1  signed out
02:45  crew 1  signed in, code
03:45  crew 1  signed out
04:15 to 06:00  the same, every hour
06:00  texts:  crew 1  30 x 7 = 210   crew 2  20 x 8 = 160
               crew 3  25 x 8 = 200   crew 4  15 x 8 = 120
               crew 5  20 x 9 = 180   crew 6  23 x 10 = 230
               total 1,100
Every sign-out came exactly one hour after a sign-in. All night.

blocks.label: crew_signins_22_october.png

diagram.aria: Thursday 22 October 2026, 00:00 to 06:00, one row per crew. Green is signed in, red is signed out. All six crews are green from 00:00 and turn red at 01:00. Crew 1 is back at 01:15, crew 2 at 01:30, crew 3 at 01:45, crew 4 at 02:00, crew 5 at 02:15, crew 6 at 02:30. Each green stretch after that lasts exactly 60 minutes and is followed by 30 minutes of red. Markers: 01:00 six calls, 02:15 crew 1 signed out again.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the desk computer's sign-in list. Green: signed in, streets marked. Red: signed out, streets emptied but not marked. Every crew turned red at 01:00, exactly an hour after signing in, and the 01:00 street was emptied but not marked. One code at a time, 15 minutes each, brought them back from 01:15 to 02:30. After that each code bought exactly 60 minutes, and each crew waited 30 minutes for the next: 50 of 144 streets unmarked, 1,100 households texted at 06:00.

blocks.text: At 06:00 my desk screen showed the night's texts: 1,100. Both changes passed their reviews. What should the council change before it happens again?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Count the minutes from each of crew 1's sign-ins to the sign-out after it. Then: what did the app do every 15 minutes on Tuesday night that it stopped doing on Wednesday night? And when each team planned its change, what did it expect the other team's part to keep doing? Ask them both.

replies.author: u/depot_desk_edurne
replies.text: Sixty minutes, every time. I phoned both teams at 08:00. The security team: "We assumed the app refreshes every 15 minutes, as it always has." The app team: "We assumed sign-ins last 24 hours, as they always have." To assume is to rely on something staying true without checking it. Neither team had written theirs down, and neither had seen the other's change.

comments.author: u/roll_it_back_olatz
comments.text: One-hour sign-ins were never needed on a bin lorry. Who steals a phone from a cab at 3 AM? Roll the security change back to 24 hours: the battery saving keeps working, and you're back to how it always was. One setting, done tonight.

replies.author: u/depot_desk_edurne
replies.text: The security team says a crew phone was left on a night bus in August. The app lists the homes where crews fetch the bin from the door, because the person living there can't wheel it out.

comments.author: u/one_signoff_thordis
comments.text: Nobody saw the whole picture, that's all. Where I work, one senior architect, the engineer whose job is how every part fits together, approves every change before it goes out. She'd have caught this in a minute.

comments.author: u/four_readers_tuulikki
comments.text: Two reviewers is thin for anything that touches sign-ins. We put four on every change. More readers, more chances someone spots the problem.

reply.prompt: The council's teams meet on Monday 26 October. What should they change about how changes are reviewed? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add more reviewers to every change, so each one is checked by more pairs of eyes first.
options.verdict: Four readers, still one change each
options.part2: From November every change got four reviewers instead of two. In the sim, replaying Wednesday night with 4 reviewers per change: the security change's four check a 1-hour sign-in against the app as it runs that day, refreshing every 15 minutes, and approve it. The app team's four check the battery saving against 24-hour sign-ins and approve it. Nobody reads both. At 01:00 all six crews are signed out, crew 1 again at 02:15, and at 06:00 1,100 texts go out, with 94 of 144 streets marked.
options.senior: More reviewers on one change find more mistakes inside that change. This mistake was in no single change: each was right about the system as it stood when it was reviewed, and the two together were wrong. Reviewers can only check what they are shown, so the fix is to show them the system as it will be, with the other changes that touch the same promise, not to add more eyes to one piece.

options.text: Have each change list what it assumes, and review it with every team relying on it.
options.part2: The council asked Vigdis, a staff engineer, to own changes that cross teams. She manages neither team. She asked for one thing first: every design doc, the written plan for a change, now ends with a list headed "Assumes". She keeps one page of shared promises, things one team's part promises the others: how long a sign-in lasts, how often the app refreshes. A change to any of them is reviewed once, with every team that relies on it, against their lists. In the sim, replaying Wednesday night with a joint review: both lists are read together before either change goes out, the clash is flagged before release, and the app team holds its change until the app keeps its 15-minute refresh during a route. Sign-ins stay at 1 hour. All six crews stay signed in, all 144 streets are marked, and 0 texts go out. Vigdis ran the first joint reviews herself, then sat beside two engineers from the app and security teams while they ran the next ones.
options.senior: Each review was right about its own change and wrong about the system, because each assumed the other team's part would keep doing what it always had. Make those assumptions visible: every design doc lists what it assumes. Then treat anything several teams rely on, such as how long a sign-in lasts or how often the app refreshes, as a shared promise, and review any change to it once, with every team that depends on it, against their lists. Someone has to own that: a staff engineer who connects teams they don't manage and teaches others to run these reviews, so it doesn't depend on one person forever.

options.text: Have one senior architect check and approve every change, before any of it goes out.
options.verdict: Trade-off: catches it, then everything waits
options.part2: The council named one senior architect to approve every change. In the sim, replaying Wednesday night with one architect: she reads both changes, sees the clash before release, and holds the app team's change. 0 texts go out. But the council's 5 software teams send about 15 changes a week and she reads about 10, so after 4 weeks 20 changes are waiting for her, and 0 of 5 teams still review their own changes. By December the app team waits two weeks for a one-line fix, and nobody else on any team has learned to spot a clash.
options.senior: One person who sees everything does catch cross-team clashes, and for a small company it can work for a while. But every change now queues behind one reader, so the architect becomes the bottleneck, and the teams stop learning to review because someone else always will. The knowledge stays in one head. A staff engineer who owns cross-team changes runs the review with the teams and mentors them, so the skill spreads instead of piling up at one desk.

options.text: Undo the security change, so sign-ins last 24 hours again, the way they always did.
options.verdict: No texts, and the old risk back
options.part2: The council rolled the security change back on Tuesday 27 October. In the sim, replaying Wednesday night with it undone: sign-ins last 24 hours, no crew is signed out, all 144 streets are marked, 0 texts. But a lost phone stays signed in for up to 24 hours again. In December crew 4's phone was left on a night bus at 00:40. It was still signed in when it turned up at 11:00, and the app's log showed it had been opened at 02:10, on the list of homes where crews fetch the bin from the door.
options.senior: Undoing one change makes the clash go away by bringing back the risk the change was made to remove. Tuesday night proved the security change works when the app refreshes. The real fault was that two teams changed two sides of one promise without ever reading each other's plans. Keep both reasons, the security and the battery, and settle them together in one review.

sim.title: Replay Wednesday night at the depot
sim.lede: You're Edurne, replaying Wednesday night, the shift from 00:00 to 06:00 on Thursday 22 October 2026, from 23:45. As given data: 6 crews sign in at 00:00, and each empties one street every 15 minutes, 24 streets a night. Households a street, crews 1 to 6: 30, 20, 25, 15, 20, 23. The app marks a street when the lorry reaches it, if its crew is signed in. Change A, the security change: sign-ins last 1 hour instead of 24. Change B, the app team's change: the app refreshes only when opened, instead of every 15 minutes; nobody opens it on a route. A code from the desk takes 15 minutes, one at a time, crews taken in the order they were signed out. At 06:00 every household on an unmarked street gets a missed-bin text. Reviews: each change in its own review, as run; a joint review, where both teams read both assumption lists before either change goes out; or one architect who approves every change. For the architect: the council's 5 software teams send about 15 changes a week and one architect reads about 10. Reviewers per change: 2, as run, or 4. Step the night in 15-minute steps.
sim.tryThis: Try this: step to 01:00. All six crews are signed out at once: 30 streets emptied, 24 marked. Step to 02:15: crew 1 is out again, an hour after its 01:15 code. Play to 06:00: 1,100 texts, 94 of 144 streets marked. Turn off change B: 0 texts. Turn off change A instead: 0 texts too, but a lost phone stays signed in for up to 24 hours. Put both back and choose the joint review: the clash is flagged before release and 0 texts go out, with sign-ins still 1 hour. Try 4 reviewers per change: still 1,100. Try one architect: 0 texts, but 20 changes waiting after 4 weeks and 0 of 5 teams reviewing. Try 5-minute codes: 372; 30-minute codes: 1,878.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the depot broke. Two changes, each approved by its own review, each assumed the other team's part would stay as it was: the security change cut sign-ins to 1 hour, counting on a refresh every 15 minutes, and the app team's change stopped that refresh, counting on 24-hour sign-ins. Together, every crew was signed out an hour after each sign-in, and 1,100 households on emptied streets were texted at 06:00.

steps.title: A sign-in and its refresh, step by step.
steps.text: A sign-in is the app's proof that a real crew lead is using it, like the wristbands in Tokens, which work until they run out. It works in four steps. First, the lead signs in with a staff number, and the council's computer gives the app a sign-in that lasts a set time; what can go wrong is a lost phone, which carries that sign-in away. Second, the sign-in lasts its time: 24 hours before Tuesday, 1 hour after; the shorter it is, the sooner a lost phone becomes useless. Third, before it runs out, the app refreshes: it asks the computer to renew it, and the time starts again; what can go wrong is a refresh that never happens. Fourth, with no refresh, the sign-in ends, and the app marks nothing until someone signs in again; here that needs a code from one desk, one at a time. Tokens covered the same pair: a short sign-in, renewed by a refresh.

steps.title: Two reviews, each right about one change.
steps.text: The security change's review checked a 1-hour sign-in against the app as it ran then: refreshing every 15 minutes, so a sign-in never got older than 15 minutes. It was right, and Tuesday night proved it: every street marked. The app team's review, held the week before, checked refresh-only-when-opened against 24-hour sign-ins, as they had always been; with 24 hours, a 6-hour shift never runs out. Nobody on the app team knew sign-ins had changed on Tuesday. Each assumed the other's old behaviour. Together, nobody opens the app on a route, so nothing refreshed: the 00:00 sign-ins ended at 01:00, and the 01:00 street was emptied but not marked. Codes took 15 minutes each, one at a time, so crews came back from 01:15 to 02:30, and each code bought exactly 60 minutes: crew 1 was out again at 02:15. After the first round each crew spent 60 minutes in and 30 minutes waiting. Streets unmarked by crew: 7, 8, 8, 8, 9 and 10, 50 of 144; times households a street, 210 + 160 + 200 + 120 + 180 + 230 = 1,100 texts.

steps.title: Review the system as it will be, not one change.
steps.text: The fix is a design review that checks the system as it will be after every change on its way out, in steps. First, every design doc, the written plan for a change, lists what it assumes: "the app refreshes every 15 minutes" is one line (Write It Down made the same case for decisions). Second, things several teams rely on, such as sign-in length and refresh, go on one page of shared promises. Third, a change to a shared promise gets one review with every team that depends on it, reading their lists together; what can go wrong is a promise nobody listed. Fourth, one staff engineer owns cross-team changes. That engineer manages neither team, so the work runs on influence without authority: asking good questions, writing the clash down so both teams see it, and earning trust. They also mentor reviewers, sitting beside them until the teams run joint reviews themselves. Larson names four kinds of staff engineer: the Tech Lead, the Architect, the Solver and the Right Hand; this job is closest to the Architect. The Second Pair of Eyes put a second reader on one change; this case puts every team that relies on a promise in one room. LATENT's a9e04, The Customer Round, is the same skill with a customer instead of a team.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail.
steps.text: More reviewers per change: in the sim, 4 instead of 2, and still 1,100 texts, because each still reads one change against today's system. Undo the security change: 0 texts, but a lost phone stays signed in for up to 24 hours, the risk the change was made to remove. Test each change harder on its own: the security change, tested with Tuesday's app, passes; the app team's change, tested with 24-hour sign-ins, passes; neither test ever runs the two together. One architect who approves everything: in the sim, 0 texts, but with 15 changes a week arriving and about 10 read, 20 are waiting after 4 weeks, and 0 of 5 teams still review their own changes. It works until she is the bottleneck, and the teams lose the skill. Faster codes at the desk only shrink the loss: 372 texts at 5 minutes a code, 1,878 at 30.

steps.title: The walk across the yard.
steps.text: At 06:40, with the last lorry back, Edurne crossed the yard to the council's offices, where she had never been past the front desk. The cleaner let her up to the second floor. The app team's room was dark; on its wall a printed page read "battery saving: approved", with two signatures and nothing about sign-ins. Down the corridor the security team's whiteboard said "sign-ins: 1 hour. Approved." with nothing about refresh. Two rooms, thirty steps apart, each sure of the other. Every code she had read down the phone all night had been made by the space between those two doors.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next shared change. The security change, sign-ins last 1 hour, assumes a refresh every 15 minutes. The app team's change, refresh only when opened, assumes 24-hour sign-ins. Both assumption lists go into one joint review with every team that relies on them, owned by a staff engineer. The review finds the clash before release and decides once: sign-ins 1 hour, and the app keeps its 15-minute refresh during a route. The crew app stays signed in all night: 0 missed-bin texts.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next shared change. Each change's design doc lists what it assumes. Because both touch one shared promise, sign-in length and refresh, they go to one joint review with every team that relies on it, owned by a staff engineer. The review finds the clash before release and decides once: sign-ins stay at 1 hour, and the app keeps its 15-minute refresh during a route. In the sim: all six crews signed in all night, 144 of 144 streets marked, 0 texts.

fix.title: The fix: written assumptions, one review per shared promise, and someone who owns it
fix.text: Every design doc ends with a list of what it assumes about other teams' parts. Keep one page of shared promises: things several teams rely on, such as how long a sign-in lasts and how often the app refreshes, each with the teams that depend on it. A change to a shared promise gets one joint review with all of those teams, reading their assumption lists side by side, before any of it goes out. Name one staff engineer to own changes that cross teams: they call the reviews, write down what was decided, and mentor engineers from each team until the teams can run joint reviews without them. For the depot, the decision is to keep both reasons: sign-ins stay at 1 hour, and the app keeps refreshing every 15 minutes while a route is running, so the battery saving still holds off shift.

limits: A joint review only catches what someone wrote down. An assumption nobody listed, or a promise nobody knew was shared, still slips through; the page of shared promises has to grow every time one is found.
Joint reviews cost time from every team involved. Kept to changes that touch a shared promise they stay rare; used for every change they become the bottleneck the architect was.
A staff engineer has no authority over the teams. If the teams' managers don't back the joint review, it becomes advice, and a team in a hurry can send its change out without it.

explain.seniorTake: Most outages between teams are not one bad change but two good ones that each assumed the other side would stay still. Reviews that read one change at a time cannot see that, however many reviewers you add. So make assumptions part of every design doc, keep a short list of the promises several teams depend on, and review any change to one of them with all of those teams at once. Leading that review is staff work: you rarely manage the people in the room, so you lead with questions, written clarity and trust, and you measure yourself by how many engineers can run the next review without you.

realWorld.title: Larson: four kinds of staff engineer
realWorld.text: Will Larson's staffeng.com names four archetypes. "The Tech Lead guides the approach and execution of a particular team." "The Architect is responsible for the direction, quality, and approach within a critical area." "The Solver digs deep into arbitrarily complex problems and finds an appropriate path forward." The Right Hand works by "borrowing their scope and authority", an executive's, "to operate particularly complex organizations." Owning cross-team changes sits closest to the Architect.

realWorld.title: Reilly: the staff engineer's three parts
realWorld.text: Tanya Reilly's The Staff Engineer's Path (O'Reilly, 2022) is about the senior engineer who leads without managing. Her own page says: "The Staff Engineer's Path has three parts: big picture thinking, project execution and leveling up." A joint review across teams is big picture thinking, and mentoring the reviewers is leveling up the people around you.

realWorld.title: Ubl: what a design review is for
realWorld.text: Malte Ubl, writing about design docs at Google in 2020, lists among their purposes: "Early identification of design issues when making changes is still cheap." And: "Ensuring consideration of cross-cutting concerns." And: "Scaling knowledge of senior engineers into the organization." A sign-in that every team relies on is a cross-cutting concern.

realWorld.title: Ubl: reviews cost something
realWorld.text: Ubl also warns: "Reviews can add a lot of value, but they are also a dangerous trap of overhead, so treat them wisely." He recalls that "When Google was a smaller company, it was customary to send designs to a single central mailing list" for senior engineers to read, a habit that stopped working as the company grew: the one-architect option at company size.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001 A.8.32: all dependencies
realWorld.text: ISMS.online's explainer of change management under ISO/IEC 27001:2022 says: "Organisations ought to map out and assess the potential effect of proposed modifications, considering all dependencies." Two changes to one sign-in, each assessed without the other, is the gap that sentence is about.

asked: How do you lead a design review across teams you don't manage?
Tell me about influencing without authority.
How do you mentor engineers through reviews?
interview.answer: I'd start by finding what the change touches that other teams rely on: a sign-in's length, a refresh, an API's shape. Anything several teams depend on is a shared promise, and a change to it gets one review with every team that relies on it, not one review per team. Before the meeting I'd ask each design doc to list what it assumes about the others' parts, and I'd read those lists side by side; most clashes show up on paper before anyone talks. In the room I don't manage anyone, so I lead with questions and writing: I state the clash in one sentence both teams agree is true, put the options and their costs in the doc, and write down the decision and who owns each part. Influence without authority is mostly that: being useful, being clear, and being trusted because you were right before and said so when you weren't. For mentoring, I run the first joint reviews myself, then sit beside an engineer from each team while they run the next ones, and hand it over. I'd tell the story of a council's refuse depot where a security change cut sign-ins to 1 hour, assuming a refresh every 15 minutes, and the app team's change stopped that refresh, assuming 24-hour sign-ins. Each review was right. Together they signed six crews out every hour and texted 1,100 households about bins that had been emptied.

atWork: Look for two changes going out in the same week that touch the same promise: a login's length and how often an app renews it, how long one program waits and how often another tries again, a message's layout and the program that reads it. Each may be approved by its own review while each assumes the other side stays as it is today; this is a common pattern behind incidents between teams. Ask three questions. Does each design doc list what it assumes about other teams' parts? Is there one written list of the promises several teams depend on, with who depends on each? When one of those changes, is there one review with every team on that list, and someone, often a staff engineer, who owns calling it? Standards, if your company is pursuing them: ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.5.6 (control of changes); Core Business Solutions' explainer says "Organizations must review and evaluate changes before implementation". ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control A.8.32 (change management), where ISMS.online's explainer says changes should be assessed "considering all dependencies." SOC 2 criterion CC8.1, which opens "The entity authorizes, designs, develops or acquires, configures, documents, tests, approves, and implements changes". A written assumption list and a recorded joint review are the evidence an auditor would look for; two separate approvals of two clashing changes are not. Build the assumption list and the shared-promise list into the first design template rather than adding them at audit time. This is not audit advice.

recall.prompt: Your company's security engineers shorten how long a login lasts in the field-service app, from 12 hours to 30 minutes; their reviewers approve it. The same week the mobile engineers stop the app renewing logins in the background, to save battery; their reviewers approve that too. Next morning, field engineers are logged out half an hour into every job and their work is lost. What went wrong, and how should reviews work from now on?

keyIdeas.idea: Each change assumed the other side's old behaviour; each was fine alone and the pair clash
Every design doc writes down what it assumes about other teams' parts
A change to a shared promise gets one review with every team that relies on it, owned by a staff engineer

recall.model: Each change was right on its own and the two clash. The security engineers assumed the app would keep renewing logins in the background, as it always had; the mobile engineers assumed logins would keep lasting 12 hours. Neither review saw the other change. From now on every design doc should list what it assumes about other teams' parts, written down where reviewers can read it. Login length and background renewal are a shared promise, so any change to either gets one joint review with every team that relies on it, reading their lists together before release, and a staff engineer owns calling those reviews.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with both changes shipped, each reviewed alone and 15-minute codes, when is crew 1 signed out for the second time, and how many missed-bin texts go out at 06:00?
recall.why: Every sign-in from 00:00 ends at 01:00 because nothing refreshes it. Crew 1 is first in line and its code ends at 01:15, which buys exactly 60 minutes, so it is out again at 02:15. Over the night 50 of 144 streets go unmarked, and their households add up to 210 + 160 + 200 + 120 + 180 + 230 = 1,100.

recall.prompt: One senior architect approving every change catches the depot's clash. Why is it the trade-off rather than the fix?
options: It doesn't catch it: one person can't read two changes
She becomes the bottleneck: changes queue behind one reader, and teams stop learning to review
Architects are not allowed to read security changes
It only works if sign-ins go back to 24 hours
recall.why: In the sim she sees both changes and 0 texts go out. But 15 changes a week arrive and she reads about 10, so 20 are waiting after 4 weeks, and 0 of 5 teams still review their own changes. A staff engineer who runs joint reviews with the teams, and mentors them, spreads the skill instead.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: how do you lead a design review across groups you don't manage, and how do you mentor engineers through it?

keyIdeas.idea: Find the shared promise and bring every team that relies on it into one review of the system as it will be
Ask every design doc to list what it assumes, and read the lists together
Lead through questions, clear writing and trust, then mentor others to run it and hand it over

recall.model: First I find what the change touches that other teams rely on, such as a login's length or an app's refresh: a shared promise. A change to it gets one review with every team that relies on it, checking the system as it will be, not one change at a time. Before we meet, each design doc lists what it assumes about the others' parts, written down, and I read the assumption lists side by side; most clashes show on paper. I manage nobody in the room, so I lead without authority: good questions, the clash stated in one sentence both sides agree with, and a written decision, which builds trust. To mentor, I run the first reviews, then sit beside an engineer from each team while they run the next, and hand it over.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The joint reviews work. Sign-ins stay at 1 hour, the app keeps its refresh on routes, and Vigdis's page lists 9 promises that several teams depend on. Then on Tuesday 12 January the maps team cut how often the lorry's position is sent, from every 10 seconds to every 60, to save on phone data. Its design doc listed what it relied on, its review approved it, and nothing on Vigdis's page mentioned position. That night, the shift starting at 00:00 on Wednesday 13 January, 8 short streets, each driven in under a minute and each with 12 households, were never marked, and 96 households got missed-bin texts. Every bin was emptied.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. The joint reviews ran as agreed. Why didn't they catch this, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The crew app relied on frequent positions but had never listed it, so the promise was not on the page and no joint review was called
Teams that rely on something must list it too, so the page grows from the users' side as well as the changers'
Add a safety net before texts go out: compare streets emptied with streets marked and hold the texts on a mismatch

coldCase.model: The joint review only covers promises someone wrote down. The maps team listed what its own change relied on, but the crew app relied on a position every few seconds to notice short streets and had never listed it, so the promise was not on Vigdis's page and no joint review was called. The fix is that teams that rely on something list it too, in their own design docs: the crew app team should add position frequency to its assumption list and to the page, so a change to it brings both teams together. And add a safety net, because the page will never be complete: before the 06:00 texts go out, compare streets emptied, from the lorry's route log, with streets marked, and hold the texts on any mismatch until someone checks: here, 8 streets of 12 households, the 96.
